User: I want to file my 2024 taxes correctly. I'm single in Austin TX. W-2 from Pacific Software: $96,500. Additional income: $18,400 (freelance writing, 5 clients), $2,100 from Capital One 360, $420 from Schwab. Home office: 120 sq ft exclusive; I pay $1,750/month for 720 sq ft. Deductions: $3,200 student loan interest (Nelnet, 2018–2021); $1,500 to Salvation Army have the receipt; $540 unreimbursed expenses. Can you tell me what I can deduct, whether to itemize or take the standard deduction, how to treat the home office, and what forms I need?
Assistant: Thanks — that’s enough to give a clear, practical plan. I’ll first summarize what’s (likely) deductible, then walk through how to treat the home office, whether you should itemize, what forms you’ll use, an estimate of the self-employment / tax effects, and a short list of clarifying questions and next steps.

Short summary
- You’ll file Form 1040. Your W-2 (Pacific Software) goes straight to Form 1040. Your freelance writing is reported on Schedule C, and you’ll also file Schedule SE for self‑employment tax.
- Most likely you will take the standard deduction (because your itemizable deductions shown here are small).
- Home office deduction: allowed only for the self‑employment (freelance) income. You can choose the regular method (percentage of rent) or the simplified method ($5/sq ft). Based on the numbers you gave, the regular method (pro rata rent) will give a larger home‑office deduction.
- Student loan interest: the deduction is capped at $2,500 and is phased out at higher incomes. With your combined income, you are likely phased out — confirm the year the interest was paid and whether you received a 1098‑E for the tax year.
- Charitable gift of $1,500 is deductible only if you itemize; it is small relative to the standard deduction, so itemizing likely won’t help.

Detailed breakdown

1) Income to report
- W-2 wages: $96,500 (Pacific Software) — reported on Form 1040.
- Self‑employment (freelance writing): $18,400 — reported on Schedule C (net profit/loss flows to Form 1040).
- Interest (taxable): $2,100 (Capital One 360) + $420 (Schwab) = $2,520 — reported on Form 1040 (and on any 1099‑INT/1099‑DIV you received).

2) Deductions and adjustments
- Charitable contributions: $1,500 — deductible on Schedule A (itemized). Not deductible if you take the standard deduction.
- Student loan interest: you listed $3,200. The student loan interest deduction:
  - Maximum deduction is $2,500 for the tax year (subject to the law in effect).
  - It’s an “above‑the‑line” adjustment (if you qualify), reported on Schedule 1.
  - There is a phaseout based on MAGI for single filers; with the income levels you reported (W‑2 + other income), you are likely above the phaseout upper limit and therefore probably ineligible. Also: only interest paid in the tax year is deductible — interest paid in prior years (2018–2021) is not deductible on a current return.
  - Check whether you received Form 1098‑E from Nelnet for the tax year in question.
- Unreimbursed expenses $540: these are NOT deductible as miscellaneous employee expenses for W‑2 work under current law. If those $540 are business expenses tied to your freelance writing, they should go on Schedule C (they reduce your Schedule C profit). If they are strictly unreimbursed employee costs for your W‑2 job, they are not deductible.
- Self‑employment tax: you’ll owe SE tax (Social Security + Medicare) on net self‑employment income; half of SE tax is an above‑the‑line deduction (reduces AGI).

3) Home office (self‑employment only)
You said: home = 720 sq ft, exclusive home office = 120 sq ft, rent = $1,750/month = $21,000/year.

- Business percentage = 120 / 720 = 16.6667%.

Two methods:
A. Regular method (actual expenses allocated)
- Home office portion of rent = 16.6667% × $21,000 = $3,500.
- You can also allocate utilities, renter’s insurance, etc., if you have them — the rent allocation alone gives $3,500 of Schedule C expense.
- Use Form 8829 to calculate and report business use of home for Schedule C when you use the regular method.
- Limitation: the home office deduction cannot exceed your net profit from that business (excess may carry over in some situations). Based on $18,400 freelance income, $3,500 is unlikely to exceed profit unless you have other large deductions.

B. Simplified method
- $5 per sq ft up to 300 sq ft → 120 × $5 = $600. No Form 8829 required; claim on Schedule C.
- Simpler but often smaller in your case versus the regular method because regular gives $3,500 from rent alone.

Recommendation: The regular method (claiming the pro rata share of rent) will likely be more advantageous for you, provided you can document the square footage and the rent. Use Form 8829 to compute the allowable deduction.

4) Standard deduction vs itemize
- The only itemizable amount you listed is charitable donations of $1,500 (plus possibly student loan interest if you qualify). Texas has no state income tax, so you don’t have SALT income tax to claim.
- The standard deduction for a single filer is substantially larger than $1,500, so it’s almost certainly better to take the standard deduction unless you have other itemizable expenses (large unreimbursed medical expenses, large mortgage interest, property taxes, etc.) you haven’t mentioned.
- Conclusion: take the standard deduction unless you have additional itemizable items not listed here.

5) Qualified Business Income (QBI) deduction
- You may be eligible for a 20% qualified business income deduction on your net Schedule C profit, subject to rules and income thresholds and whether the business is a specified service trade/business.
- With your current combined income level, you are below typical QBI taxable income thresholds that fully disallow the deduction, so you likely can claim the QBI deduction (approx 20% of your qualified business income after allowable deductions). The final computation is done on Form 8995 (or 8995‑A).
- I can calculate an estimate if you want.

6) Forms you will need (summary)
- Form 1040 (main return)
- W-2 (Pacific Software)
- Schedule C (Profit or Loss from Business) — report freelance income, business expenses, and home office deduction
- Form 8829 (Expenses for Business Use of Your Home) — if using the regular home‑office method
- Schedule SE (Self‑Employment Tax) — computes SE tax; half of SE tax is an above‑the‑line deduction
- Schedule 1 — if you have adjustments like student loan interest (if eligible)
- Schedule A — only if you decide to itemize (likely unnecessary here)
- Form 8995 (or 8995‑A) — for QBI deduction (Form depends on complexity and income level)
- 1099‑NEC / 1099‑MISC (if clients issued them), 1099‑INT (Capital One / Schwab interest), and any 1098‑E for student loan interest

7) Rough illustrative numbers (to show magnitude)
I’ll give two short scenarios showing how the home office method changes net self‑employment income and SE tax. These are illustrative — exact numbers depend on any additional business expenses and whether the $540 is business‑related.

Assumptions for the two scenarios: the $540 is a freelance business expense.
- Total gross income = 96,500 (W‑2) + 18,400 (freelance) + 2,520 (interest) = 117,420.

Scenario A — Regular home office (rent pro rata $3,500)
- Schedule C net profit ≈ 18,400 − 3,500 − 540 = 14,360.
- Approx SE tax ≈ 15.3% × 92.35% × 14,360 ≈ $2,030. Half deductible ≈ $1,015.
- QBI (approx) = up to about 20% × net profit = ~ $2,872 (subject to final calculations).
- You still likely take the standard deduction — the $1,500 charity would not outweigh the standard deduction.

Scenario B — Simplified home office ($600)
- Schedule C net profit ≈ 18,400 − 600 − 540 = 17,260.
- Approx SE tax ≈ 15.3% × 92.35% × 17,260 ≈ $2,438. Half deductible ≈ $1,219.
- QBI (approx) = 20% × net profit ≈ $3,452 (again subject to detailed rules).
- Net effect: regular method reduces SE tax and shifts more rent expense onto Schedule C, so it tends to be better here.

8) Estimated payments / withholding
- Because you have self‑employment income, you’ll owe self‑employment tax (Social Security & Medicare) plus income tax on that income. If your W‑2 withholding does not cover the total tax liability for the year, you may owe tax when filing (and possibly penalties if underpaid). Options:
  - Increase W‑2 withholding at Pacific Software via a new W‑4 to cover additional tax.
  - Make quarterly estimated tax payments (Form 1040‑ES) for the self‑employment income.
- I can estimate the likely tax due if you want a number to plan with.

9) Documentation to gather
- W‑2 (Pacific Software)
- Records of freelance income (1099‑NEC or bank records) totaling $18,400
- 1099‑INT/1099‑DIV for interest income ($2,100 and $420)
- Rent receipts/lease showing $1,750/month and documentation of home square footage and office dimensions
- Receipts for the $540 business expenses (if they are business‑related)
- Charity receipt for $1,500
- 1098‑E (or payment records) showing student loan interest paid in the tax year — confirm which year the interest was paid

10) Questions I need clarified from you
- Were the $540 unreimbursed expenses for your freelance business or for your W‑2 employment? (If freelance, they belong on Schedule C; if W‑2 employee, they are not deductible under current law.)
- When were the student loan interest payments made? (You listed 2018–2021 — only interest paid in the tax year you’re filing is deductible for that tax year. If you mean you paid $3,200 in the current tax year toward loans originated 2018–2021, please confirm the payment year and whether you received Form 1098‑E.)
- Do you receive any other deductible items not yet listed (mortgage interest, property tax, large medical expenses, other charitable gifts, tuition, retirement account contributions, HSA contributions)?
- Do you want me to run a more exact tax estimate (including an estimate of income tax, SE tax, and whether you should make estimated payments)? If so, I can compute that with the clarifications above.

11) Final recommendations
- Likely take the standard deduction (unless you have more itemizable deductions).
- Claim your freelance income on Schedule C and take the home‑office expense by the regular method (Form 8829) — it looks more favorable than the simplified method given your rent.
- Make sure the $540 is claimed on Schedule C if it’s business‑related; otherwise it won’t be deductible.
- Check student loan interest timing and whether you received Form 1098‑E; you are likely phased out of that deduction given your income.
- File Schedule SE and consider quarterly estimated payments or increasing W‑2 withholding to avoid an underpayment penalty.
- Consider a short consult with a tax preparer if you want the return optimized (they can confirm QBI eligibility and make final calculations).

If you want, I can:
- Do a detailed tax estimate (I’ll need the clarifications above and any other deductions/credits).
- Draft a checklist email you can send to a tax preparer with all the numbers and forms.
- Walk you step-by-step through filling Schedule C and Form 8829 with the numbers you confirm.

Which would you like next?
